Solution
Words: 175
i OurBigBook.com
Two integrations by parts give the boundary form of the Sturm-Liouville operator:
⟨f,Lg⟩−⟨Lf,g⟩=[p(f′∗g−f∗g′)]ab​.
(1)
The interior terms cancel because p,q are real. Thus the required endpoint condition is
[p(f′∗g−f∗g′)]ab​=0for every f,g in the operator domain.​
(2)
For a regular interval, a standard self-adjoint domain is specified by one real homogeneous Robin boundary condition at each endpoint:
Aa​y(a)+Ba​p(a)y′(a)=0,Ab​y(b)+Bb​p(b)y′(b)=0,
(3)
where neither pair of real constants is identically zero. At each end, these conditions force the two boundary data vectors of f,g to be proportional, making the displayed form zero. Dirichlet boundary conditions and Neumann boundary conditions are the cases B=0 and A=0. Coupled conditions also work, for example y(a)=y(b) and p(a)y′(a)=p(b)y′(b), whose two endpoint contributions cancel. Self-adjointness uses the maximal common domain with these conditions, not an arbitrary smaller symmetric restriction.
The weighted inner product must be nondegenerate. The usual interpretation is w>0 almost everywhere, allowing isolated endpoint zeros as in part (b), with the operator defined on its appropriate weighted domain. Merely allowing a weight that is zero on an entire interval would not by itself define the stated operator or a positive-definite inner product on ordinary functions.

Words: 57
ii OurBigBook.com
Let Lϕ=λϕ with ϕ=0 in the self-adjoint domain. By the boundary identity from part (i),
λ⟨ϕ,ϕ⟩=⟨ϕ,Lϕ⟩=⟨Lϕ,ϕ⟩=λ∗⟨ϕ,ϕ⟩.
(4)
Since its squared weighted norm is positive, λ∈R​.
For Lϕn​=λn​ϕn​ and Lϕm​=λm​ϕm​, the same identity gives
λn​⟨ϕm​,ϕn​⟩=λm​⟨ϕm​,ϕn​⟩.
(5)
Thus λn​=λm​ implies
∫ab​ϕm∗​(x)ϕn​(x)w(x)dx=0.​
(6)
This is orthogonality of Sturm-Liouville eigenfunctions. Degenerate eigenspaces can be given an orthonormal basis, although vectors in a degenerate eigenspace are not automatically orthogonal.

iii OurBigBook.com
Choose a complete orthonormal system of eigenfunctions ϕn​ for the self-adjoint problem. Expand f=∑n​fn​ϕn​ and y=∑n​cn​ϕn​, with
fn​=⟨ϕn​,f⟩=∫ab​ϕn∗​(ξ)f(ξ)w(ξ)dξ.
(7)
Substitution into Ly=f gives λn​cn​=fn​. Since no eigenvalue is zero, the Sturm-Liouville eigenfunction expansion is
y(x)=n∑​λn​ϕn​(x)​∫ab​ϕn∗​(ξ)f(ξ)w(ξ)dξ.​
(8)
For eigenfunctions not normalized to one, divide each term additionally by ⟨ϕn​,ϕn​⟩. The expansion is understood in the weighted function space and, with sufficient data regularity, in the operator domain. A zero eigenvalue would instead require its corresponding source coefficient to vanish and would leave an arbitrary homogeneous component.

Expanding the general Sturm-Liouville form gives
Ly=−wp​y′′−wp′​y′+wq​y.
(9)
Matching the second-derivative coefficients requires p/w=x−4. Matching the first-derivative coefficients then gives p′/p=−2/x. Up to a common positive normalization of p,q,w, one may therefore take
p(x)=x−2,w(x)=x2,q(x)=−ax2.​
(10)
Indeed −x−2(x−2y′)′−ay=−x−4y′′+2x−5y′−ay. The left endpoint is singular in these coordinates. Its self-adjoint interpretation is supplied by the regular transformed problem in part (ii), rather than by assuming that p(0) is finite.

Set z=x3/3 and write y(x)=Y(z). Then
y′=x2Yz​,y′′=2xYz​+x4Yzz​,
(11)
so the two first-derivative contributions cancel exactly, leaving
−Yzz​−aY=λY,Y(0)=Y(1/3)=0.
(12)
The Dirichlet spectrum of −d2/dz2 on this interval is (3nπ)2, n≥1. If λ+a≤0, the linear or hyperbolic solutions cannot satisfy both zero endpoints nontrivially, so no additional modes have been omitted. Thus
λn​=9n2π2−a,yn​(x)=6​sin(nπx3),n=1,2,….​
(13)
To verify normalization, use dz=x2dx:
∫01​x2sin(nπx3)sin(mπx3)dx=∫01/3​sin(3nπz)sin(3mπz)dz=6δnm​​.
(14)
This proves weighted orthonormality and also transfers completeness from the ordinary Fourier sine series. The construction is the cubic-coordinate reduction of a singular Sturm-Liouville operator. The positive constant a shifts the entire spectrum down; a zero eigenvalue occurs if a=9n2π2, so the no-zero-eigenvalue proviso in part (a)(iii) must be imposed separately if that inverse formula is used here.

a OurBigBook.com
Suppose Ψ1​ and Ψ2​ have the same boundary data, and put u=Ψ1​−Ψ2​. Then Δu=0 in V and u=0 on its boundary. For real u, the product rule for the divergence gives
∇⋅(u∇u)=∣∇u∣2+uΔu=∣∇u∣2.
(15)
The divergence theorem therefore yields
∫V​∣∇u∣2dV=∫S​u∂n​udS=0.
(16)
The nonnegative integrand must vanish, so ∇u=0 throughout V. On each connected component u is constant, and its zero boundary value makes that constant zero. Hence Ψ1​=Ψ2​​, proving uniqueness. For complex fields, apply the same argument to real and imaginary parts, or use ∇⋅(u∗∇u) and its real part.
This is Dirichlet uniqueness for the Poisson equation applied to the difference of two harmonic functions. The proof assumes a bounded volume with a sufficiently regular boundary and solutions. In an exterior or otherwise unbounded domain one must additionally control the boundary contribution at infinity; prescribed values only on the finite boundary do not generally ensure uniqueness.

For Φ=X(x)Y(y), separation of variables gives X′′/X+Y′′/Y=−(m2+p2). With the standard separation constants m2 and p2, the zero-endpoint solutions are sines. Thus, provided mp=0,
Φ(x,y)=sin(mx)sin(py)​
(17)
is nonzero, has zero value on all four sides, and satisfies ΔΦ=−(m2+p2)Φ.
There is a missing qualification in the printed request for arbitrary integer m,p. The Dirichlet and Neumann spectra of a square show that a nonzero Dirichlet solution exists precisely when
m2+p2=j2+k2for some integers j,k≥1.
(18)
When one of m,p is zero, the displayed sine product vanishes identically, and a nonzero solution need not exist: for example (m,p)=(0,0) or (0,1) admits none. On the other hand (0,5) does admit sin(3x)sin(4y). Thus the natural intended case is two nonzero integer indices, with the stated spectral criterion covering the exceptional cases.

ii OurBigBook.com
Choose the separated cosine solutions instead:
Φ(x,y)=cos(mx)cos(py).​
(19)
Its derivatives are Φx​=−msin(mx)cos(py) and Φy​=−pcos(mx)sin(py). They vanish on the appropriate opposite sides of the square for integer m,p, so the outward normal derivative is zero everywhere on the boundary. Also ΔΦ=−(m2+p2)Φ.
This is nonzero for every pair of integer indices, including a zero index. For m=p=0 it is the constant solution, illustrating the zero mode allowed by Neumann boundary conditions. Negative indices give the same cosine modes. The construction is the Neumann part of the Dirichlet and Neumann spectra of a square.

For the real decaying Bessel form used here, take k>0. The original PDF has Km​(r) as the last factor in its auxiliary differential equation, although both differentiated factors have argument kr; that last argument must also be kr for the stated Modified Bessel differential equation.
Put B(r)=Km​(kr). The corrected identity is B′′=−B′/r+(k2+m2/r2)B. Since the field is radial, the radial Laplacian gives
(Δ−k2)(r−pB)​=r−p[B′′+r2−2p​B′+(r2p(p−1)​−k2)B]=r−p[r1−2p​B′+r2p(p−1)+m2​B].​
(20)
Away from the point source this must vanish. For k>0, a constant ratio of rB′ to B would make B a pure power, incompatible with the k2r2 term of its equation. Therefore both displayed coefficients must vanish:
p=21​,m2=41​,so m=±21​.​
(21)
The two orders give the same Modified Bessel function of the second kind: K−1/2​(z)=K1/2​(z)=π/(2z)​e−z.[ref]
The source describes k merely as real, but the following displayed real square-root formula implicitly needs k>0. For the operator with arbitrary real k, its decaying fundamental solution instead uses κ=∣k∣; k=0 is obtained by a limit. The unmodified real AKm​(kr) ansatz is not a real Bessel formula for all negative k.

Write C=Aπ/(2k)​, so the radial field is Φ=Ce−kr/r. Integrate its equation over a ball of radius ϵ centred at the source. The divergence theorem gives
4πϵ2Φ′(ϵ)−k2∫r<ϵ​ΦdV=1.
(22)
The second term is 4πk2C∫0ϵ​re−krdr=O(ϵ2) and vanishes in the limit. Meanwhile
4πϵ2Φ′(ϵ)=−4πC(1+kϵ)e−kϵ⟶−4πC.
(23)
Thus
C=−4π1​,A=−4π1​π2k​​,Φ(r)=−4πre−kr​.​
(24)
The minus sign follows from the convention (Δ−k2)Φ=δ(3), opposite to the positive static Yukawa Green function for −Δ+k2. For arbitrary real k, replace it in the exponential by ∣k∣ to select decay at infinity. The k=0 limit is −1/(4πr).

Solution

Words: 102
c OurBigBook.com
Reflect the source across the plane, defining r′∗=(x′,y′,−z′) for an interior point z′>0. Superpose the direct Green function from part (b) and an image of opposite sign:
Ψ(r,r′)=−4π1​[∣r−r′∣e−κ∣r−r′∣​−∣r−r′∗∣e−κ∣r−r′∗∣​],κ=∣k∣.​
(25)
The direct term supplies the delta source in the upper half-space; the image singularity lies outside that domain and contributes no source there. On z=0 the two distances are equal, so the terms cancel, giving homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions. Both decay at infinity, which is the additional condition selecting this half-space solution. This is the method of images realization of the Dirichlet image kernel for the three-dimensional modified Helmholtz equation. It includes the unscreened case k=0.

Let f=u+iv be analytic on a neighbourhood of a bounded planar region Ω and its piecewise smooth boundary C, oriented with Ω on the left. The Cauchy integral theorem states
∮C​f(z)dz=0.​
(26)
For a region with holes, C includes the clockwise inner boundaries as well as the counterclockwise outer one. In particular, the integral around a closed contour bounding a region throughout which f is analytic is zero.
To prove this classical form, expand the line integral and apply Green's theorem to its real and imaginary parts:
∮C​fdz​=∮C​(udx−vdy)+i∮C​(vdx+udy)=∬Ω​(−vx​−uy​)dxdy+i∬Ω​(ux​−vy​)dxdy.​
(27)
Both integrands vanish by the Cauchy-Riemann equations, ux​=vy​ and uy​=−vx​. Analyticity supplies the continuous first partial derivatives needed by this Green's theorem proof. The requirement that the enclosed region contain no singularities is essential.

Put s=1/n, so 0<s<1. For the complex exponentiation zs, choose −π/2<argz<3π/2: the branch cut is the negative imaginary axis. Integrate zs/(a2+z2) around the upper half-plane semicircle, with a small semicircular indentation excluding the origin. The only enclosed simple pole is z=ia, with residue
Resz=ia​a2+z2zs​=2ia(ia)s​.
(28)
The large arc is O(Rs−1) and the small arc is O(ϵs+1), so both vanish. On the negative real segment, zs=eiπs∣z∣s; accounting for the direction of traversal, the two real segments therefore sum to (1+eiπs)I, where I is the desired positive-axis integral. The residue theorem gives
(1+eiπs)I=πas−1eiπs/2.
(29)
Since 1+eiπs=2eiπs/2cos(πs/2),
I=2cos[π/(2n)]πa1/n−1​.​
(30)
The endpoint estimates also prove convergence. More generally the same calculation is the fractional-power integral from an upper-half-plane contour, valid for −1<s<1.

Set z=eiθ. Then dθ=dz/(iz) and tanθ=(z2−1)/[i(z2+1)], so the requested integral is
I=i1​∮∣z∣=1​f(z)dz,f(z)=z[a2(1+z2)2−(1−z2)2](1+z2)2​.
(31)
The denominator factors as
[(a−1)+(a+1)z2][(a+1)+(a−1)z2].
(32)
For 0<a<1, its two inner roots are z=±r, r=(1−a)/(1+a)​<1, and the other two roots have modulus 1/r>1. There is also a simple pole at zero. Their residues are
Res0​f=a2−11​,Res±r​f=2a(1−a2)1​.
(33)
The latter values follow by differentiating the quadratic product, or from the supplied hint. The sum of the enclosed residues is
−1−a21​+a(1−a2)1​=a(1+a)1​.
(34)
The residue theorem therefore gives
I=a(1+a)2π​,C=2π.​
(35)
At the angles where the tangent is undefined, the original reciprocal has a removable zero limit. Its continuous extension gives the same integral; the transformed rational integrand has no pole on the unit circle.

f​1​(ω)=2πδ(ω−ω0​).​

Writing the sine as (eiω0​t−e−iω0​t)/(2i) then gives
f​2​(ω)=iπ​[δ(ω−ω0​)−δ(ω+ω0​)].​

These are tempered distributions, since the time-domain functions are not integrable on the full real line. The second formula also correctly vanishes when ω0​=0.

F−1(f​∗g​)(t)​=2π1​∫R​∫R​f​(η)g​(ω−η)eiωtdηdω=2π1​[∫R​f​(η)eiηtdη][∫R​g​(ν)eiνtdν]=2πf(t)g(t)​.​

The reciprocal in this transform must mean the principal-value reciprocal distribution. Its inverse transform is
F−1(PVω1​)(t)​=πi​∫0∞​ωsin(ωt)​dω=2i​sgnt,​
(39)
using the given Dirichlet integral and the sign of t. Also F−1[δ](t)=1/(2π). The inverse of the proposed expression is consequently (iA/2)sgnt+B/(2π). Comparison with H(t)=[1+sgnt]/2 for t=0 gives
A=−i,B=π,H(ω)=−iPVω1​+πδ(ω).​
(40)
The value assigned at the single point t=0 does not affect the distribution. This is the Fourier transform of the Heaviside step function; treating 1/ω as an ordinary integral would miss the required prescription.

∫0L​y​xx​sin(kn​x)dx=−kn2​∫0L​y​sin(kn​x)dx.
(45)
The delta source contributes F(ω)sin(kn​x0​). Multiplying by 2/L and using the coefficient definition therefore yields
(kn2​−ω2)bn​(ω)=L2​sin(kn​x0​)F(ω).

Away from the resonant frequencies this gives
bn​(ω)=αn​kn2​−ω2F(ω)​,αn​=L2​sin(kn​x0​).​

Expand in the complete Fourier sine series y​(ω,x)=∑n≥1​bn​(ω)sin(kn​x) and apply Fourier inversion. Substitution of part (ii) gives
y(t,x)=πL1​n=1∑∞​sin(kn​x0​)sin(kn​x)∫−∞∞​kn2​−ω2F(ω)eiωt​dω,C=πL1​.​

To check the source normalization, apply ∂t2​−∂x2​ mode by mode. It cancels the denominator; the remaining inverse transform gives 2πF(t), and completeness gives
L2​∑n≥1​sin(kn​x0​)sin(kn​x)=δ(x−x0​).
(49)
The endpoints vanish termwise. These identities establish the equation in the distributional sense, with classical validity wherever the series and derivatives converge suitably.
The displayed real-axis integrals in the paper are not ordinary convergent integrals at their poles. One definite choice is the Cauchy principal value at each ω=±kn​. If a causal solution is wanted, use [kn2​−(ω−i0)2]−1 instead. Its inverse transform is H(t)sin(kn​t)/kn​, so the causal solution is
yret​(t,x)=L2​∑n≥1​kn​sin(kn​x0​)sin(kn​x)​∫−∞t​F(s)sin[kn​(t−s)]ds,
(50)
when the past integral exists. The principal-value choice instead uses the time-symmetric kernel sin(kn​∣t∣)/(2kn​). No temporal initial data are given, so homogeneous sine and cosine modes remain permissible additions. This is the causal Fourier resolvent of a point-driven fixed string.

Under the specified passive change of orthonormal basis, each Cartesian tensor index acquires one copy of L. Thus a tensor of order n transforms as
Sa1​⋯an​′​=La1​b1​​⋯Lan​bn​​Sb1​⋯bn​​.​
(51)
Repeated old-basis indices are summed from one to three. Orthogonality of the new basis gives LLT=I. Taking determinants yields (detL)2=1, hence detL=+1 or −1​. The positive case preserves orientation and the negative case reverses it.

Solution

ii OurBigBook.com
A pseudotensor has an additional determinant factor under an orthogonal transformation. Thus its rank-three transformation law is
ϵijk′​=(detL)Lia​Ljb​Lkc​ϵabc​.
(52)
The contracted expression Lia​Ljb​Lkc​ϵabc​ is fully antisymmetric in i,j,k, so it equals a scalar multiple of ϵijk​. For (i,j,k)=(1,2,3) it is precisely the determinant expansion of L, fixing that scalar to detL. Therefore
ϵijk′​=(detL)2ϵijk​=ϵijk​.​
(53)
The Levi-Civita symbol consequently has the same numerical entries in every orthonormal frame when interpreted as a pseudotensor. With an ordinary rank-three tensor transformation law alone it would instead acquire a minus sign under an orientation-reversing transformation.

Integrating the Dirac delta distribution in x3​ reduces the inertia integral to the planar lamina. Use u=x1​−x2​, v=x2​, so x1​=u+v and the parallelogram becomes the square −D≤u,v≤D, with unit Jacobian determinant. The mass is M=4σD2, and symmetry gives a centre of mass at the origin.
Odd rectangular integrals vanish. The required second moments are

I=34σD4​​1−10​−120​003​​=3MD2​​1−10​−120​003​​.​

The off-diagonal entries are minus the product moment, not the product moment itself. This is the unit-shear case of the inertia tensor of a sheared rectangular lamina.

Expand the tridiagonal determinant along its first row. The diagonal entry contributes dDN−1​. In the off-diagonal cofactor, expansion along its first column supplies the other factor −k, and the cofactor sign makes the net contribution −k2DN−2​. Therefore
DN​=dDN−1​−k2DN−2​,N≥2.​
(66)
The initial values are D1​=d and D2​=d2−k2. Writing the same formula at N=2 forces D0​=1​, the empty determinant convention. This is the tridiagonal determinant recurrence.

Substitute DN​=βN into the recurrence. Since k>0, its roots are nonzero and satisfy
β2−dβ+k2=0,β1​+β2​=d,β1​β2​=k2.​

For distinct roots, the general recurrence solution is DN​=c1​β1N​+c2​β2N​. The initial values require c1​+c2​=1 and c1​β1​+c2​β2​=d=β1​+β2​, giving
c1​=β1​−β2​β1​​,c2​=−β1​−β2​β2​​,DN​=β1​−β2​β1N+1​−β2N+1​​.​
(68)
At a repeated root, d=±2k and β1​=β2​=β=±k, this quotient must be replaced by its limit:
DN​=(N+1)βN.​
(69)
It also follows by solving the repeated-root recurrence as (c1​+c2​N)βN. This exceptional case is necessary to avoid introducing a false root in the next part; it is included in the fixed-end spring-chain determinant and its repeated-root limit.

The ratio one is excluded: at that repeated root, part (iii) gives (N+1)(±k)N=0. Thus the naive extra root corresponding to equal recurrence roots is spurious.
To count the physical solutions without ambiguity from exchanging β1​ and β2​, write β1,2​=ke±iq and d=2kcosq with 0<q<π. Then
DN​=kNsinqsin[(N+1)q]​.

Write B(x) for the displayed matrix. The hyperbolic addition identities give
B(x)B(y)=(cosh(x+y)−sinh(x+y)​−sinh(x+y)cosh(x+y)​)=B(x+y).
(73)
Thus matrix multiplication is closed in G. It is associative because ordinary matrix multiplication is associative. The identity is B(0)=I, and B(x)B(−x)=I gives the inverse B(x)−1=B(−x). Hence G is a group​.
Moreover, x↦B(x) is an injective homomorphism from the additive real numbers, since sinhx determines x. Therefore G≅(R,+)​; in particular it is abelian. These matrices are the connected boost subgroup relevant to the component quotient of the real Lorentz group in two dimensions.

For a subgroup N≤H and h∈H, a left coset is hN={hn:n∈N} and a right coset is Nh={nh:n∈N}. A normal subgroup satisfies hNh−1=N for every h∈H, equivalently hN=Nh.
If N is normal, the quotient group is the set H/N of cosets, with multiplication
(hN)(kN)=(hk)N.​
(74)
To check independence of representatives, replace h,k by hn1​,kn2​. Then
(hn1​)(kn2​)=hk(k−1n1​k)n2​∈hkN,
(75)
because normality puts k−1n1​k in N. Thus the operation is well defined. Associativity follows from that in H, the identity is N, and the inverse of hN is h−1N. This proves the group axioms for H/N and explains the role of coset multiplication is well-defined exactly for normal subgroups.

Direct multiplication gives T2=P2=I, TP=PT=−I, and
TB(x)T=PB(x)P=B(−x).
(76)
Thus conjugation by each generator of G′ preserves G; so does conjugation by every product of the generators. Therefore G⊴G′​.
Using TB(x)=B(−x)T and its analogue for P, every group word can be reduced to B(x)S with S∈{I,T,P,TP}. Consequently the quotient has at most four cosets. They are distinct: a nonidentity diagonal matrix among T,P,−I cannot equal B(x), since a diagonal B(x) requires sinhx=0 and hence B(x)=I. Therefore
G′/G={G,TG,PG,TPG}.
(77)
The three nonidentity cosets all square to G, and TG and PG commute because T,P commute. Hence
G′/G≅C2​×C2​,the Klein four-group.​
(78)
Equivalently, G′ is the full real O(1,1) group and G its identity component. This is the component quotient of the real Lorentz group in two dimensions; the quotient records the four components, not the continuous boost parameter.

a OurBigBook.com
The relation mR=R−1m moves every reflection factor to the right of every rotation factor. Canceling pairs m2=I and reducing rotation powers modulo n shows that every word has one of the forms
Dn​={Rj:0≤j<n} ∪ {Rjm:0≤j<n}.​
(81)
Within either family the elements are distinct, since equality would imply equality of two powers of R, which has order n. No rotation equals a reflection: in the polygon action, rotations preserve planar orientation and reflections reverse it. Thus this complete list has exactly 2n elements.
Geometrically, R rotates the polygon by 2π/n about its centre, and m reflects it in a symmetry axis through the centre. The elements Rj are all rotations; Rjm are all reflections. We use the paper's convention that Dn​ has order 2n, since another common convention calls this same group D2n​.

b

Words: 178 Articles: 1
9 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 178
b OurBigBook.com
Rotations commute with one another, while reflection conjugation sends Rj to R−j. Thus the rotational conjugacy classes are pairs {Rj,R−j}, except when the two entries coincide. For reflections, direct use of the relations gives
Rs(Rjm)R−s=Rj+2sm,m(Rjm)m−1=R−jm.
(82)
If n is odd, multiplication by two permutes residues modulo n, so all reflections are conjugate. The complete class list is
{I};{Rj,R−j} (1≤j≤(n−1)/2);{Rjm:0≤j<n}.​
(83)
Their sizes are 1, then (n−1)/2 classes of size two, then one class of size n, giving (n+3)/2 classes and 2n elements in total.
If n is even, the half-turn Rn/2 is central and forms its own singleton. Conjugation changes a reflection exponent by an even amount or negates it, so it preserves parity and reaches every exponent of that parity. The list is
{I},{Rn/2};{Rj,R−j} (1≤j<n/2);{R2jm:0≤j<n/2},{R2j+1m:0≤j<n/2}.​​
(84)
There are n/2+3 classes; their sizes are 1,1, then n/2−1 pairs, then two classes of size n/2. Geometrically the two reflection classes correspond to vertex-axis and edge-axis reflections, in either order depending on the choice of m. These are the conjugacy classes of a finite dihedral group.

Let n=p≥3 be prime. Any subgroup contained in ⟨R⟩≅Cp​ is either {I} or the whole rotation subgroup. Both are normal: the trivial subgroup always is, and the rotation subgroup has index two, or equivalently is preserved by mRm−1=R−1.
If a normal subgroup contains any reflection, it contains its entire conjugacy class. Part (b) shows that this is every reflection for odd p. Products of reflections include a generator of the rotations, since (Rm)m=R. Such a normal subgroup must therefore be the whole dihedral group.
Thus the complete list of proper normal subgroups, including the trivial subgroup, is
{I}and⟨R⟩={I,R,…,Rp−1}.​
(85)
This also agrees with classification of subgroups of a dihedral group: the reflection subgroups of order two are proper but are not normal when p is odd.

a OurBigBook.com
Work over the complex numbers, the usual scalar field for the finite-group character theory used below. A group representation on a nonzero vector space V is a homomorphism D:G→GL(V), so D(gh)=D(g)D(h) and D(e)=I.
A faithful representation is injective: distinct group elements have distinct representing maps. Equivalently, its kernel is just {e}.
An irreducible representation has no nonzero proper invariant subspace: if W⊆V and D(g)W⊆W for every g∈G, then W={0} or W=V. Irreducibility concerns invariant subspaces, whereas faithfulness concerns whether any group element is represented by the identity.

D(g−1)=[D(g)]−1.​
(87)
If only multiplicativity is initially stated, D(e)2=D(e) together with invertibility of representation matrices first implies D(e)=I. This explains why a group representation takes values in the general linear group rather than arbitrary square matrices.

The elements 1,−1 commute with the whole quaternion group, so they form singleton classes. Each of the three remaining pairs is a conjugacy class: for example conjugation by j sends i to −i, and likewise cyclically. No such pair can mix with a different pair, because the quotient by {±1} is abelian and its cosets {±i}, {±j}, {±k} are preserved by conjugation. Hence
{1},{−1},{i,−i},{j,−j},{k,−k}.​
(88)
For a finite group over C, the number of inequivalent irreducible representations equals the number of conjugacy classes, so there are five. The sum of squares of irreducible representation dimensions is the group order, eight. With five positive integer dimensions, the only possibility is
1,1,1,1,2.​
(89)
Indeed five one-dimensional contributions give five, and replacing one by a two-dimensional contribution adds exactly three; any further enlargement would exceed eight. These are the dimensions used in the character table of the quaternion group.

For the remaining two-dimensional character χ2​, its value at the identity is two. Column orthogonality between the identity and −1 gives 4+2χ2​(−1)=0, so χ2​(−1)=−2. Between the identity and each of the other classes, the four linear-character values sum to zero, forcing the remaining character values to vanish. Thus the character table is
class sizeχ++​χ+−​χ−+​χ−−​χ2​​{1}111112​{−1}11111−2​{±i}211−1−10​{±j}21−11−10​{±k}21−1−110​​.​

The choice of scalar field matters here, even though the displayed matrices are real. Over R, this particular four-dimensional representation is irreducible: for any nonzero real vector v, the vectors v,D(i)v,D(j)v,D(k)v are mutually orthogonal with the same nonzero norm. This follows from the skew-symmetry and quaternion multiplication identities of the three matrices. A nonzero invariant real subspace contains all four vectors and is therefore the whole space.
